storylines.label: Inference Fast
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Resin, fast native scheduler for LLM inference engines

editorial.tldr: Prime Intellect launched Prime Inference on Oct 8 as a hosted serving option for frontier open models. On Oct 21 the vLLM blog introduced Humming, a quantized-inference kernel library from Ant Group and the vLLM community.
editorial.whats_new: Resin, a native scheduler for LLM inference engines, appeared as a Show HN on Oct 26, extending the speed push from hosted serving and kernels to scheduling.
editorial.why_it_matters: Inference speed work is now landing at three layers (hosted serving, kernels, scheduling), so latency gains can come from swapping a layer instead of changing models.
editorial.take_for_builders: Benchmark Humming on your own quantized models and GPUs before adopting it, and treat Resin as an experiment until it publishes comparisons.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Moonshot AI resets Kimi K3.1 Pro quotas after user complaints

editorial.tldr: On Oct 16, coverage framed Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 as a name without a released model, and one report said a new Chinese export-license requirement for large AI models could affect it. On Oct 23, reports said it was being readied for release after Arena testing.
editorial.whats_new: On Oct 26, TradingView reported Moonshot AI reset Kimi K3.1 Pro quotas after user complaints, following the Oct 24 launch coverage of the Pro model.
editorial.why_it_matters: Quota resets after complaints signal usage limits on the new Pro tier are still unsettled, which affects capacity planning and reliability for anything routed to it.
editorial.take_for_builders: Rerun your own evals on Kimi K3.1 Pro before routing traffic, and keep a fallback model until Moonshot's quota limits and license terms are confirmed stable.

status.detail: Kimi K3.1 Pro is now covered as launched, with a Pro Highspeed API reported, but Moonshot had to reset quotas after user complaints.

storylines.label: Their Own
storylines.latest_title: Why founders keep failing to vibecode their own LLM inference engine

editorial.tldr: "Their Own" groups four items that share a phrase, not one developing event. They run from an Oct 14 paper on distilling web agents from black-box teachers to an Oct 21 study of models rewriting their own harness and an Oct 23 study of whether models trust their own justifications.
editorial.whats_new: A Startup Fortune piece on Oct 24 argues founders keep failing when they try to vibecode their own LLM inference engine; only the headline was available, so its evidence is unverified.
editorial.why_it_matters: All four touch the build-versus-depend question for agent stacks: distill a cheaper agent, let the model tune its own scaffold, trust its own explanations, or write your own serving layer. None yet gives production evidence.
editorial.take_for_builders: Do not replace a maintained inference server (vLLM, SGLang or a hosted API) with a self-written engine on the strength of this piece; keep the existing stack until a source shows benchmarked results.

status.detail: Four unrelated items sharing a phrase; no single event is unfolding.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

editorial.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of RL items, not one developing story. Since Oct 12 it has collected a Qwen long-horizon agent report, an O-RAN benchmark, and four Oct 20-22 arXiv papers on training tool-using and search agents.
editorial.whats_new: Oct 23: three more arXiv papers land, on aligning rounding between inference and training for stable LLM RL, RL-trained user simulators for task-oriented dialogue, and the RobustRLlib robust-RL benchmark, beside AWS's SageMaker guide.
editorial.why_it_matters: The Oct 23 rounding-location paper targets a training-stability failure: separate inference and training systems can make an intended on-policy update off-policy even with identical weights and BF16 tensors. The SageMaker guide remains the only managed-platform recipe; QwenGyre (secondary-source report) and X-RIC stay research or telecom-specific.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you train LLMs with separate inference and training stacks, check rounding-location alignment as a cause of on-policy drift; if you run on AWS, try the SageMaker Wordle pipeline before planning around it, and wait for Qwen's primary QwenGyre release.

status.detail: A loose set of RL items; the newest add training-stability, simulation and robustness work alongside the AWS guide.

storylines.label: Typed Decision
storylines.latest_title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox

editorial.tldr: Typed decision models return a probability over caller-defined options instead of generating text, and papers began placing them in agent systems as guardrails. The first paper showed an attack on that role; a security-triage study followed.
editorial.whats_new: A paper on routing a personal multilingual inbox compares typed decision models against a classical baseline and a generative LLM, arguing to measure before training.
editorial.why_it_matters: Typed decision heads are being proposed as guardrails and routers, so platform engineers need to know both how they can be attacked and how they compare with simpler baselines.
editorial.take_for_builders: If a typed decision model gates agent actions, test its option definitions for adversarial wording and benchmark it against a classical baseline before training.

status.detail: Three papers in 15 days cover an attack, a security-triage application, and a baseline comparison for typed decision models.

storylines.label: Claude 5.5
storylines.latest_title: Kimi K3.1 Pro vs. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra

editorial.tldr: Latent Space's Oct 7 newsletter put Claude Haiku 5.5 ahead of GPT-6 Luna at the same pricing. On Oct 20, Google Cloud added Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to its Antigravity coding tool.
editorial.whats_new: R&D World compares Kimi K3.1 Pro against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra (Oct 23); only the headline is in the item, so the results are not confirmed here.
editorial.why_it_matters: Claude 5.5 models are reaching more surfaces (Antigravity), and a Chinese open-weight lab is now being benchmarked against Opus 5.5, so model-routing choices are being re-opened.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you route between models, rerun your own evals with Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro as candidates before changing defaults, and treat the Haiku 5.5 vs Luna claim as unverified until you test it.

status.detail: Claude 5.5 models are spreading to new platforms while Kimi K3.1 Pro is being compared against them; no outcome is confirmed in these items.

storylines.label: Machine Learning
storylines.latest_title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control

editorial.tldr: On Oct 21, a paper on extracting materials data from literature with ML and LLMs appeared alongside NVIDIA's Kumo Relational, which claims to beat supervised ML on relational data with no training. The thread is loosely linked by the 'machine learning' label rather than a single event.
editorial.whats_new: A tutorial on physics-constrained ML (Oct 23) presents a modular framework for hybrid modeling, optimization and control that builds domain constraints into models.
editorial.why_it_matters: Two items push ML toward less task-specific training (LLM extraction, training-free relational prediction); the third pushes toward encoding first-principles constraints. Both change what you build versus buy.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adopting Kumo Relational, rerun it against your own supervised baseline on your relational data; treat the claim as unverified until you do.

storylines.label: Policy Optimization
storylines.latest_title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection

editorial.tldr: On Oct 14 a paper proposed Lifted State Policy Optimization to credit the local change that turns a flawed reasoning state into a better one. On Oct 22 ReflectPO applied reflection-guided policy optimization to long-horizon LLM agents.
editorial.whats_new: SOPO (Oct 23) applies Socratic guided policy optimization to span-level hallucination detection in LLM output.
editorial.why_it_matters: Three arXiv papers in ten days tailor policy optimization to self-correction, agent horizons and hallucination detection; all are preprints, so treat them as research signals, not production tooling.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as preprints: wait for released code and independent replication before changing any training or eval pipeline.

storylines.label: On-Policy Distillation
storylines.latest_title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation

editorial.tldr: Three arXiv papers from Oct 14–22 apply on-policy distillation (training a student on its own sampled trajectories, scored by a teacher) to different problems: machine translation, long-horizon coding agents, and the question of when the teacher should lead.
editorial.whats_new: Oct 22: an arXiv paper proposes advantage-based on-policy distillation, deciding per step when the student should follow the teacher.
editorial.why_it_matters: On-policy distillation is spreading from general post-training into narrow jobs (translation, coding agents), so teams distilling small models should compare it against SFT on their own trajectories.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you distill small models, run an on-policy versus SFT comparison on your own task trajectories before adopting either method; none of these papers has independent replication yet.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: An Empirical Study of Recent Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph to Text Generation on Standard Benchmarks

editorial.tldr: This page groups items by the shared phrase "large language models"; they do not form one developing story. Oct 6–21 items cover speculative-decoding security, knowledge-graph work, sycophancy, code-translation hallucinations, search agents, and materials extraction.
editorial.whats_new: Oct 22 adds a spectral-intervention paper, an empirical KG-to-text benchmark, and a Bashkir parameter-efficient adaptation suite; none extends earlier items.
editorial.why_it_matters: Treat this as a reading list, not a thread: the useful items for platform engineers are the speculative-decoding attack surface and code-translation hallucination mitigations.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run speculative decoding in production, read the Oct 6 security paper and check whether your draft model is an untrusted input; skip the rest unless it matches your domain.

storylines.label: Empirical Study
storylines.latest_title: An Empirical Study of Recent Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph to Text Generation on Standard Benchmarks

editorial.tldr: Five unrelated arXiv papers share only the phrase "empirical study" in their titles; this is not one developing story. They span clinical-protocol coding agents (Oct 13), attack triage (Oct 21), UML hallucinations, Vietnamese classification, and KG-to-text (Oct 22).
editorial.whats_new: Oct 22 adds a UML-diagram hallucination taxonomy and a Vietnamese decision-model transfer study alongside the KG-to-text benchmark.
editorial.why_it_matters: No shared finding links these papers; the hallucination taxonomy for generated UML is the one most relevant to teams using LLMs for design artifacts.
editorial.take_for_builders: Skip unless a paper matches your domain; if you generate UML or design docs with an LLM, check the hallucination taxonomy against your own outputs.

storylines.label: Action Reasoning
storylines.latest_title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action

editorial.tldr: Three arXiv papers in three days examine the gap between LLM reasoning and acting. One proposes a benchmark for action and plan safety in embodied agents, and another tests frontier models on robot manipulation.
editorial.whats_new: A new arXiv paper formalizes the harness between an LLM and its tools as a Petri-net supervisory controller to block unsafe tool calls under prompt injection.
editorial.why_it_matters: These are research preprints, not products, but they point at where agent safety work is heading: checking actions at the execution layer rather than trusting the model's reasoning.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agents call tools, treat the execution layer as the place for enforcement; these preprints are unreplicated, so test any approach on your own tool set before relying on it.
